utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. If there are no procedural matters, we -- Mr. McCloskey, I see you on your feet. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. Just briefly as I think everyone knows -- and could we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal. Please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. There are also in this trial protective measures in place for you. You will not be addressed by your real name but by a pseudonym, and now Mr. Vanderpuye for the Prosecution is commencing his examination-in-chief. You have the floor, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Witness. I'd like to show you -- I'd like to show you 65 ter 7539, and if you would please just take a look at that and confirm that you're the person named in this document without telling us your name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be on the screen in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, are you able to confirm that that's your name that appears in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My surname, my last name, is correct, but there's a mistake in the first letter. Otherwise, everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should try to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The first letter that you refer to, is that -- should the first letter be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, we should go into private session, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document 65 ter 7539 will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7539 marked in court by the witness shall be assigned Exhibit P2650, admitted under seal. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall having testified in the case of Prosecutor versus Popovic on the 10th and 11th of January, 2007?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember having testified during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to -- one moment. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President, but Mr. Tolimir has -- is experiencing some technical problem. He can't hear properly through his headset. He cannot hear the witness. He can hear everybody else in the courtroom but not the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This problem should be resolved first. Court usher is assisting. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I propose that the witness say something so that we can check to see if Mr. Tolimir is receiving him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think everything is in order now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you should just continue and Mr. Tolimir's invited to indicate immediately if there are any problems with the interpretation or receiving the original language.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you again, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, have you had an opportunity to listen to your testimony before testifying here today, that is, your Popovic testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have had that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And having listened to your Popovic testimony, do you stand by it; that is, would you give the same answers to the same questions if they are put to you in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as possible, I would confirm everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to offer into evidence the witness's prior testimony, which is 65 ter 7537 under seal and 7538, together with the associated exhibits that were tendered through him in that proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The transcript of the Popovic trial will be received, the former one under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7537 shall be assigned can be number P2651, admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The other documents in the list which were admitted in the Popovic trial will be received as well. That means the long list starting with 65 ter 1667 through 65 ter 75 -- no, sorry. Mr. Vanderpuye, you should clarify which of those should be part of this so-called Popovic package, especially as I see some documents with a little star and the indication that they were not yet on the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. All of those documents were tendered through the witness, that's through 7549 -- yes, through 7549. The ones with the star were not on the 65 ter list originally. Those are documents that were tendered through the -- or by the Defence in the other proceeding, and so they weren't originally part of our 65 ter list, but they do constitute part and parcel of his testimony. For that reason, we're tendering them as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the usual question again. Do you have any objections to add the documents used in the Popovic trial but not yet in the 65 ter exhibit list to the 65 ter exhibit list of the Prosecution? That means the documents 65 ter from 7540 through 7549. Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May there be peace in this house, and may God's wishes be done and not my wish. I would like to welcome the witness in our midst. We have no problem to have that adopted, to have the Popovic document adopted. So we have no objection, and the Prosecutor is free to proceed as he sees fit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to add these documents to the 65 ter exhibit list, and all those will be received as exhibits. The best way to put P numbers to them is by internal memorandum by the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The transcripts of the testimony of the witness in the Popovic case will be received, 65 ter 7537 under seal, and we want to have the P number now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 7537 has been assigned P2651 under seal, and the redacted one 65 ter document 7538 shall be assigned Exhibit P2652. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the other documents will get a P number by an internal memorandum. Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have a brief summary of the witness's testimony I'd like to read into the record. The witness adopted his OTP witness statement of 5 May 1999 and provided the following evidence on the 10th and 11th of January, 2007, in the Popovic case. I'll need to go into private session for a moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The witness testified that there were between two and five workstations the intercept operators of the northern site used and described in detail the procedures and protocols they followed. The witness described how he would listen to radio intercepts and recorded important conversations. The taped conversations were transcribed into notebooks as soon as practicable after the tapes were reviewed, sometimes multiple times if necessary. The notebooks were then given to a designated typist or cryptographer who was responsible for entering the transcribed conversations into a computer and sending it off electronically to the 2nd Corps command. New notebooks were generally not opened until the circulating notebooks were full. Prior to February 1995, intercepts were transcribed on pieces of paper rather than notebooks at the northern site. The interception process was prioritised. For example, conversations involving VRS generals were considered important, whereas those involving ordinary citizens tended not to yield as good information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should slow down a little bit, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The witness testified that as a rule, everything said during a conversation was written down. Summaries were rare. However, as important information sometimes needed to be extracted from apparently unimportant conversations, brief summaries were made. Also in very urgent situations, information was relayed directly over a wire communication -- a wire connection or even open telephone lines. The witness described how intercepts were marked. For example, he noted that "as a rule, if something is in brackets and if there is a question mark, then the person transcribing had doubts as to the identity of that person and would ascribe another sign to that person, namely an X." Through his experience the witness was sometimes able to identify the voices of the individuals he intercepted, including Vinko Pandurevic and Generals Simic, Zivanovic, and Tolimir. Finally, the witness identified 29 handwritten intercepts as his own. Mr. President, that concludes my summary, and I have a few additional questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like an explanation, namely on page 7, line 23, the Prosecutor said that the witness accepted the statement given on the 9th -- on the 5th of May, but I don't see it on the Prosecution list. Is that an omission or was that statement not accepted and admitted in the Popovic trial, because following the Popovic trial, they had a different practice. It was only subsequently that they admitted documents into evidence. So I'd just like an explanation from Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it's on our exhibit list, it may not be, but in any event, it's on the first page of the transcript concerning his Popovic testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have read the transcript from this witness's testimony in the Popovic trial, but I see that we haven't dealt with this witness's statement. So it's not on my list, at least as far as I can see. On the Prosecution list, that is. If I'm wrong, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You may be right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My point is you may be right, that it might not be on the exhibit list, and if it isn't that's an omission, but the statement itself is directly and specifically referenced in the transcript of the testimony. What I've read is a summary of that testimony, and so if there's any uncertainty as to whether or not the witness said what he -- what he did about his statement, that can be found in the first page of his testimony in Popovic case which Mr. Gajic has indicated that he's read. If there's an omission in the exhibit list, I will remedy that by providing that -- that -- that exhibit. If it was admitted. It may not have been, but it was specifically referred to nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you referring to the OTP -- witness statement of 5th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You may proceed, and we will see whether or not you will use this or not or if the Defence will use it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You may have noticed that it is referred to in the statements of the witness that is appended to the exhibit list, and I think that's quite explicit in that list. It's just a question of whether or not it appears also in the category of exhibits that were admitted through the witness, which I don't believe it does, but like I said that's probably just an omission that needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, it is the first item in the attachment to the exhibit list to be used with the witness by the Prosecution. Without a 65 ter number but with the ERN numbers and the date of disclosure in English and B/C/S to the Defence. Please go ahead, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll need to go into private session for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Vanderpuye, that you're tendering 65 ter 3045E, but not A.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would actually like to tender all versions of it, Mr. President. They are A and E, and they are the same intercept. One is a handwritten, and one is a printout version of that intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Both versions will be received as exhibits. That one with a letter E under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3045E shall be assigned Exhibit P2653, admitted under seal. And 65 ter document 3045A shall be assigned Exhibit P2654. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, when we met yesterday, did you have an opportunity to look over five intercepts that were shown to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw copies of those intercepts in my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And would those have been intercepts that you took down during the course and scope of your duties and responsibilities as an intercept operator back in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The copies I saw correspond to my handwriting and the manner in which we wrote down the intercepted conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like you to do if you could, and you'll let me know if it's necessary, is take a look at tabs 1 through 5, the very last ones in the binder that I indicated before, and from that point on -- and take a look and see if you can recognise your handwriting in the intercepts that are contained under each of those tabs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Except for one tab where the handwriting belongs to another colleague, all the rest are in my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And which tab are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In tab 3, the handwriting is that of a colleague of mine above my handwriting, so part of that document is in my handwriting. Yes. And there's another page before that. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Is the page before that in your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President, tabs 1 through 5 are 65 ter numbers -- I think we've just received tab 2. We've just gotten a P number for. So it's 65 ter number 3475, and then we have A and C -- B and C, and then we have the tab 2 which was just admitted in evidence, then we have P2488. That's tab 3, which consists of -- oh. I see we have -- and also I'd like to tender 65 ter 3070D, which is the printout under that tab of the intercept. And then we have under tab 4 -- under tab 4 we have 65 ter 3107A and C, and under tab 5, 65 ter 3108A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have finished with reading the numbers of those documents you want to have -- having been admitted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: So these documents under tab 1, 3, 4, 5, will be admitted into evidence, but I will read the numbers into the transcript, because the registrar doesn't have a binder. Firstly, 65 ter 347B -- sorry, again. 65 ter 3475B and C will be received as exhibits, the first one under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3475B shall be assigned Exhibit P2655, admitted under seal. And the 65 ter document 3475C shall and assigned Exhibit P2656. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. 65 ter 3107A and C will be received as exhibits, the latter one under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3107A shall be assigned Exhibit 2657. And 65 ter document 3107C shall be assigned Exhibit P2658, admitted under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We continue 65 ter 3108A and B will be received as exhibits, the latter one end seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 3108A shall be assigned Exhibit P2659. And the 65 ter document 3108B shall be assigned Exhibit P2660, admitted under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And lastly -- and lastly, the Exhibit 65 ter 3070D will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 3070D shall be assigned Exhibit P2661, admitted under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure if we have already received the other two under tab 2. I think so, but I'm not sure. We should check that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I believe we did receive that just a moment ago. It's been given P2654 and P2653 respectively. That's A and E versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you indeed. Then we have this resolved, and I just would like to put on the record the reason for admission of these documents. The witness has confirmed that he saw in the original document his handwriting, except one part of one page. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to show the witness 65 -- well, I think we have an exhibit number now. It's tab 1. 65 ter -- I'm sorry, P2656 -- yeah, P2656 is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to draw your attention to -- I think we're waiting for the translation. Yes. To the entry here indicated at channel 11 21:43, and we can see here an indication that this is a conversation between an individual named Krsmanovic and someone named Toso. First, are you familiar with those names? Can you recall those names in the context of your work back then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there are many names I can't recall, and I can't recall these names either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, with respect to this particular intercept, it says that Krsmanovic, in a conversation or "discussion with Toso about the problem of transportation that Krsmanovic mentioned 10 buses and 14 trucks in relation to the means that are not requisitioned." And then in quotes it says: "That was the situation today." First, is this an example of a summary of an intercepted communication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a rule, this is a conversation which was probably not especially important, so what might have been interesting for our command was extracted from it. If a conversation is evaluated as unimportant but there's something that might be useful in it, then that bit is extracted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you a printout of this conversation, which is P2655, and you'll see it under tab 1. You'll see the typewritten version of this conversation at the third page of that typewritten --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- transcript. First let me start with the top -- with this document that's on the screen, page 1, which indicates the location and the date of 16 July 1995. The report number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you should wait until we have the English translation on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And again, it should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm not sure that the caption of the document has been translated. I think only the intercept has been translated in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In any event you can see at the top it says Armija Republika Bosne i Hercegovine, and then it says the command of the 2nd Corps, and then it indicates the location case which we've not -- which we haven't referred to directly, because it's -- then you can see the date of 16 July 1995, and then the report number which is 25/16795. Below that we can see the time of the first intercept in this report series at 19:41 hours. And if we go to page 3 of the document in the B/C/S, we will see an entry for 21:43, channel 9 [sic], which is the conversation that we just saw, it's at the bottom of the page, that we just saw in your handwriting a few moments ago. So with respect to this particular intercept, would it be correct to say that it was recorded -- I mean, written down by you close in time to when the conversation actually occurred?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 20, line 8, it says "channel 9." However, as far as I can see, at least from the printed version I have here on the screen, it's channel 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It should be channel 11. It's channel 11 in the handwritten, and it should be channel 11 in the printout which I think we can all see, so perhaps it's just an error in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The other possibility is that you misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: A very remote one, but thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that this conversation would have been transcribed, that is written down by you, close in time to when the conversation itself occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that is the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And would that have been given to the typist and inputted in the computer to generate this typewritten information on the date that's reflected in the caption of this report, that is, the 16th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the practice. Information would be given to the communications guy on duty to be forwarded to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And just so that I'm clear anyway, the reference here to Toso, do you have a recollection of who that would have been or who that was back then in July 1995, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall. It escapes me at the moment. I don't know who the person was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I just have one more document to show you, and that's -- and that's P773. Just a moment and I'll give you the handwritten -- P773B, please. That should be the handwritten version of this intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where can we find it in the binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President. Just a moment, and I'll ... You will find that under tab 25, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Here we have an intercept from the 22nd of July, 1995. It's timed at 9:28 hours, and it indicates that this is a conversation between Popovic, it says X, and General Tolimir. In this conversation we can see that P is looking for General Tolimir and X says that he's right next to him. P asks to speak to him and says, "This is Popovic." And then we can see the transition and apparently T gets -- Tolimir gets on the phone. And we have a conversation that ensues where Popovic is trying to find out some information concerning a relative of his so that he can tell the family something. Do you have a present recollection of who the Popovic is that's in this -- is a speaker in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's been a long time, so I don't remember either the participants in the conversation or the details of it, so I can only assume, which isn't very helpful to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the General Tolimir that's indicated here, do you have a present recollection about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several conversations, as far as I remember, where the general appeared, either himself or he was -- people asked to speak to him, but I don't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: But in any case, the General Tolimir that's referred to here, I take it, was a VRS officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a very important person as far as we were concerned, those of us who intercepted these conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we go to the second page in the B/C/S, we can see here at the top of the page that Popovic is trying to get certain information, and lower down on the page we can see that General Tolimir asks him how things are going, and we can see that Popovic's response is that there are no problems, and he says that he's at his base. He also says that there's some business to be finished. And if we go to the next page in English, and I think we can go down the page in the B/C/S. We'll see that General Tolimir tells him to just do his job. And if we go to the next page, I think, in the B/C/S, we may see the same thing. Has it -- let me ask it this way: Did -- did you have information about a Popovic VRS officer while you were doing this particular function? Did you know of any particular Popovic VRS officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. There were many officers. I don't remember Popovic specifically. Perhaps if we talked at the time, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you just a couple of questions and then we'll be finished. Were you aware of any Popovic that worked in the Drina Corps of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew -- well, I heard, whether then or later, I had heard of the man who led the Bratunac Brigade, and I heard a conversation somewhere in the evening at around 8.00 when this man was engaged in a conversation. He'd come back from the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, thank you very much, Witness. I appreciate your testimony, and that concludes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vanderpuye. Sir, now Mr. Tolimir has the opportunity to put questions to you during his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to greet all those present once again, the witness, too, and wish him a pleasant stay here with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could you tell us, please, in this summary here and in your answers, we could see that you went to some sort of course, attended a course, before you started working in the unit -- in the Anti-Electronic Warfare Unit as Mr. Vanderpuye said during his examination-in-chief. Is that correct? And could you tell us what that course was and how long it lasted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I arrived in the unit in August 1994, and I started working before the course got going. The course started sometime in the second half of September and went on for the first half of October of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, please, whether that was the only course you attended, or did you have any additional training in some other unit, perhaps, or in your corps or outside your corps, or outside the army, for that matter? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was no other training, just that course which was organised in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether, having done your military service, you were sent to any other training courses abroad or outside Bosnia-Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Having done my military service, I was a member -- well, that was my obligation in the Territorial Defence and later on civilian protection, but I didn't go anywhere else. I didn't go abroad with respect to the establishment in the Territorial Defence and civilian protection system.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us now whether you have tapes of those 29 conversations that you were shown and that you transcribed in your own hand? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe tapes like that exist. Perhaps some tape might still remain, but they were used again. They were deleted. So I doubt very much whether the tapes of those 29 conversations exist. Perhaps there were some earlier tapes before, before 1995, but I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, please, whether you were shown during the proofing session with Mr. Vanderpuye, when he showed you the conversations, whether there was someone from the chain of command above you who used those transcripts, the ones that you transcribed in your own hand? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, linked to the chain of command on the ground on my shift I was the person who was, if I can put it that way, in charge, the first person in the chain of command in that process. So nobody else looked at that -- at those transcriptions, but when it did go to the command, I didn't have any feedback information. So that is just linked to my own handwritten transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, of the transcripts that you were shown here which are originals and the Prosecutor showed you, on any of those conversations that you transcribed in your own handwriting were -- were there any initials by any of the users of the information up the chain of command above you? Did anybody initial any of those transcripts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't see any markings like that, any signature or initials. There was just this -- the signature of the signalsman who forwarded this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Vanderpuye showed you a document of a conversation between Krsmanovic and Toso, and I quote -- I forgot to make a note of the tab. It's tab 3. Krsmanovic says in a discussion about the problems of transport with the participant Toso, "he mentioned some 10 buses and 14 trucks, 9 with regard to -- well, things that have not been mobilised," and then that's the end of the quotation, and then in brackets it says, "That was the case today," in inverted commas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I think it's another tab. Could you assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's tab 1, Exhibit P2656.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Aleksandar. I apologise if you weren't able to follow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So let's look at tab 1 now, document P2656. Was that the right number? So if you could read that and then I'll ask you a question. Would you be able to identify this person Toso and Krsmanovic on the basis of this note on their conversation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who these people are. The conversation is so short that I don't believe I can say any more than that. I really don't know who those two men were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But if the Court were to establish -- need to establish who these people are, could you identify the participants given a description? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say any more than I've already said and any more than is written here. They introduced themselves. They said what they said. I transcribed and took note of what they said, and that's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is this a summary of what they said or is it direct speech? Is it their direct speech or related speech?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I see that we have both, a quotation and a summary. So it's a combination of the two. The inverted commas were quotation, and I had to round it off for the command so that they could understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us what the quoted part of the conversation is and which participant in the conversation uttered those words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In brackets is the quotation. Now, since I did not conduct a detailed analysis, I assume it was Mr. Krsmanovic who said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that your assumption or can you claim that with certainty? And on the basis of this related conversation, can we actually ever establish who said what? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This isn't a conversation that was conducted in the usual procedure. Well, not conversation. I mean transcription. The transcription wasn't made according to standard procedure, so we can't see who said what. So it's difficult to identify anything. This is just my assumption, and I can no longer remember who said what, actually. We see what it says here, and that's the best I can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, are there any conversations which you were shown here at the Tribunal as transcripts of the source that there is -- that was initialled by the user of the information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen any such conversation here. Well, I apologise. Let me be more precise. You said in the original version. In the original version, I have never seen anything like that except some handwriting and some additional figures, numbers. Otherwise, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm not going to say your name because you're a protected witness. Thank you for coming here to testify today. The Defence has no further questions four. May God bless you and I wish you bon voyage back home.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence rests. We have further questions for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes already your examination here in this trial. Now you are free to return to your normal activities and go home. The Chamber would like to thank you for coming here to The Hague and for assisting us. The court usher will assist you in leaving the courtroom. We go into closed session for a moment to enable you to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye, I see you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I had a chance to look over the exhibit sheet in relation to the statement that Mr. Gajic was remarking about, and I did find it, actually, on there. It's already admitted in this case under P839, and it's on page 9 of the exhibit sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Correct. I found it as well. It's under seal. Mr. Gajic, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no reason to believe Mr. Vanderpuye. I assume there must be a list. I probably have a different list because one, two, or three lists have circulated, so quite possibly I have a previous list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I take it that you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "I have no reason not to believe Mr. Vanderpuye." Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, this is what I thought you would have said. As always in this trial, that's a common understanding and a good trust. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes. I was misinterpreted. What I said was I have no reason not to believe Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There are also a number of -- on page 11 of the exhibit sheet, we have a number of notebooks, full notebooks, that have been MFI'd. I don't see that there's any reason to tender those fully. We don't have translations for the entire notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We are not intending to translate the entire notebook because we don't think that it's necessary in order for the purposes of -- for the purposes of their admissibility. I don't know if the Defence has a problem with that, but -- so if that's an obstacle to their admission, then so be it, but we still think that they're admissible for the purposes for which they were tendered. Some of them were tendered simply because of what they depicted on the cover or to establish that there were registration numbers in the notebooks and so on and which we don't think need -- requires the translation of the entire notebook in order for them to be admissible. So it's our intention not to translate them in their entirety and -- but I understand that they were marked for identification pending translation of the entire book. So I think that's an issue that I will discuss with Mr. Gajic to see whether or not he has any objection to that, but I think otherwise our position would be -- or we would request that they be admitted without the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you haven't used these documents with the witness or with any other witness, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. Have we used this documents with other witnesses? Was that the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No. This is -- in that part of your list where you say "used with the witness but admitted with other witnesses in prior proceedings."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means it was not used with the last witness who was testifying today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And therefore we have no formal ground to admit them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is the reason why I raise it. The -- the ground for their -- their admission through evidence -- I have to actually determine what witness they came in through, but I thought I would address it because it is on his -- on his sheet, and obviously we don't have any other intercept operators coming to testify in this case. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So I thought it would be important to address it. Perhaps we can reach some sort of an understanding with the Defence with respect to whether or not -- whether or not all of these will require translation. I don't believe that they do, because I think they were either admitted or used under very limited purposes or for limited purposes. In any event, we don't believe that we need them translated fully, because some of them contain hundreds of intercepts, in order to establish the purpose for which they were admitted. I raise it now because it's on his sheet. I understand they were also admitted in the prior case through PW-041 who was a witness in this case as well. There were circumstances under which -- there were extenuating circumstances with respect to that witness's testimony, which may also explain why those documents weren't used with him. If we can go into private session, I can explain that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Since we don't have another witness for today, I assume, there is no. We should take the opportunity to continue our hearing after the break, because there are some reasons for -- to discuss procedural matters, how to proceed in this trial, but we should have a slightly longer break to enable the Chamber to consider the situation, and I think we should have our break now and resume at 11.30, and perhaps the Prosecution is in a position to update us in relation to the last witness. We adjourn and resume half past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This part of today's hearing is only to deal with procedural matters. Mr. McCloskey, do we have any more information in relation to the remaining witness? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber now wants to deal with the matter of scheduling for the remainder of the case. First of all, the Chamber expects that the Prosecution closes its case after the completion of the possible testimony of the final witness who was scheduled for this week. The Chamber is considering the views of the parties with respect to the planning of the remainder of the case and will be issuing a Scheduling Order setting out specific deadlines and dates shortly. Before doing so, however, the Chamber would like to give an indication to the parties of its current intentions. The Chamber envisions to order the Defence to file the following on the 1st of December or earlier: A list of witnesses and the nature of these witnesses, their 65 ter summaries, and the points in the indictment to which the witness will testify; the estimated length required for each witness and the total time for the Defence case; the 65 ter exhibit list; the list of expert witnesses and the accompanying curriculum vitae and reports of those witnesses; any Rule 92 bis, ter, or quater motions. The Chamber envisions further that there will and pre-Defence conference the first day after the break, that is, on the 9th of January, 2012, with any opening statement, and the first witness to follow immediately thereafter. Finally, the Chamber envisions to hold a Status Conference on the 5th of December in order to review the progress between the parties. I would now like to ask the parties if they have any position with respect to this possible scheduling which the Chamber has in mind. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That sounds fine with the Prosecution. I think that's -- that's more than -- more than reasonable, and is no problem from our perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm happy to hear that the Chamber has handed down its decision more or less as we requested, so I would like to thank the Chamber for its understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. However, to clarify, this was not the order, the final order, it was just information given by the Chamber about the intentions of the Chamber, but a written decision will follow in due course. If there are no objections, no additional submissions, we can leave it like it is. Mr. Gajic, anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we would just like to receive some information about the next witness, when that witness might possibly appear in court, because we have to plan our activities. There's a lot of work awaiting the Defence. This legal assistant or advisor has to travel to Belgrade. So what is the time period in which we will learn whether the witness will appear or not and be certain if he's not coming that he's not coming? We would be very grateful to the Prosecution if they could tell us something about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, we adjourn until further notice without an indication of a new day of hearing. That will be pronounced in the normal way. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do have some information that I think will help the Court and the parties in planning. If you want to take -- it shouldn't take me more than a few minutes. It's related to when you'd asked us if there was a point where the Defence and the Prosecution could get together and decide about other issues, and much of this I -- we have now identified, and we do need to meet with Mr. Gajic on, but I can tell you just -- because there's a few outstanding issues that we owe you information on, and if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And related to intercepts, as the Court is aware, we have many intercepts in this case that it's been the Prosecution's strategy and position to call the intercept supervisors so that you would understand the intercepts from the big picture and to call individual intercept operators that had important intercepts, many of which were acts and conduct under that rule. As you are aware, that leaves many other intercepts where no intercept operator has testified but that are relevant, important intercepts to this case, and what we traditionally have done in all the cases, as we intend to do here, is file a motion to introduce those other intercepts under 89(C) since that we have -- it's -- we base this largely on the practice of business records is -- is what I would compare it to, and that since you have now seen the process, you know how it works, you know that these materials were done in a certain way at a time related to their date and that under 89(C) you would now have the ability to allow these other intercepts into evidence to help give a -- give a complete package of Srebrenica intercepts, and what we have -- will have for you along with that motion is an index of the intercepts, basically mostly starting in July, working our way through August 1st. Well, you may remember the last few intercepts talk about people going across the river. And so you have an index with a little summary of the intercepts, the time, the people that are speaking on them. And so you have right in front of you the historical chronology of the intercepts that would reflect the intercepts that are in evidence and the ones that we're offering into evidence. We wait until the end here so that we know which intercepts we don't have to offer into evidence because so many are in. So I just wanted to alert you. We do plan on filing that very, very soon, that -- that intercept motion. Also, you may recall that we've -- we have a trial video that is in evidence that was a compilation of various videos and that we've seen testimony from Erin Gallagher and I think Dusan Janc on additional video. So we have a new trial video that has a few additions. If you recall, General Tolimir pointed out some information on one of the Zepa videos that we had left out that he thought was relevant, so we've included that. It had some reference to some family members, and that is -- the trial video I'm speaking of is P991. So we do have a new updated trial video that includes those various pieces that have actually already into evidence so that you will get, ideally, the DVDs with that on it and a transcript in English. The audio is, of course, B/C/S, so we have not transcribed it as yet. So -- and along with that new trial video, updated trial video, really, is a book, an updated stills book, and that is the book that goes along with each chapter of the trial video and has a few stills from each chapter to give you a feeling of who's in the video and who they are. It's really a crucial guide to watching the video, because it tells you -- it reminds you who people are, and, you know, it's as important as the playbill or -- at a football game or the opera, really. So we have an updated version of that that we'd like to provide for you, and the original one was P1097. And also there's a couple of items that were MFI'd, the statement of Dr. Klonowski which I will need to speak to the Defence about. I don't know if you remember that but that was something that may have been in dispute, so we'll try to sort out where we are on that. There was another MFI'd only a -- something that we recovered from the Bratunac Brigade called: "The Situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina Before the War," and I think you'd asked us about the authenticity of that and so that's another document, it's a war history document. I need to -- that's P1258. Does that mean it's in evidence? It's MFI'd only. That I need to talk to Mr. Gajic about to see their opinion on. Oh, and we also have an updated Muslim identification book. You may recall Ms. Gallagher testifying about stills taken of Muslims in Potocari and along the road, and we have an updated version of that based on her testimony identifying people, and that is P1367. So that update should reflect her testimony. And there may be a couple of other things that the team is digging up that I'll be able to sit down and discuss with Mr. Gajic and get back to you and perhaps we'll be able to set some time if we need to to have any argument if -- if we need to or -- or decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you get the floor, one moment, please, Mr. Gajic. I would like to add that recently I asked the parties if they could -- could agree on certain pages of one book which was tendered during an examination of one witness to avoid to having translate everything of this book. Mr. Gajic, it seems that you want it address that. Otherwise, I would like to ask Mr. McCloskey first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic picked out some 20-some-odd pages that we were fine with and so that will go off to CLSS under the agreement that you suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have to decide which pages should be received into evidence. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't receive interpretation at the moment. Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, now I can hear the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was saying the Defence has pinpointed some 25 pages, I think, from the book, and it will be sent, if it hasn't been sent already, but I did discuss the matter with Mr. McCloskey. I don't know whether I provided him with a copy, but I will do so, if not, in the course of the day. Now, as far as what Mr. McCloskey told us about the Prosecution intentions for submitting new material and having new exhibits admitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Bear with me for one moment. The Chamber asked the parties to give us an update about the -- your agreement about the pages to be translated and to be received into evidence. The Chamber decides about the admission of evidence. So we have to be updated to be able to decide. Can you give us the page numbers now? That would be extremely helpful so that we can resolve this already today. Could you read the numbers into the transcript, including the number of the document, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we do that by means of e-mail, because I don't have the page numbers with me at present, but as soon as this session is over, I will be able to send that in writing, because the pages are clearly marked, but I don't have the numbers with me at present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I can indicate that the Chamber will receive these pages into evidence, but without having the page numbers, it's quite difficult to identify later, at a later stage, which are in evidence. Yes, please do that after the hearing. At least during the final session of the Prosecution case we can deal with that finally. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Secondly, Mr. President, I have to admit that Mr. McCloskey took me by surprise with the amount of exhibits that he would like to have tendered and the amount of work we're going to have, because the Defence can't agree in a blanket terms to everything. We'll have to look through all the material and consider it. So I'd like to ask the Trial Chamber and Mr. McCloskey to have everything in writing. If we could do that in writing, that the Prosecution table its request in writing, and then we would respond in writing during the deadline, requisite deadline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the moment I only can say I state that one witness was now formally withdrawn. I don't want to mention his name because it was in private session. The second witness, we are expecting a motion, and there might be a response and then we will decide. And all the other motions, we are open to receive any motion. There is nothing -- and, of course, the Defence will have the opportunity to respond, and at a certain stage we will decide on that. There's nothing to do with that at the moment during the hearing of today. Are there any other matters? I don't see anybody on his feet, so that we have to adjourn for the day. We will give notice when we may have the next hearing with the last witness of the Prosecution case, and I would like to take the opportunity to thank everybody who is assisting us and supporting us and was busy with us during the whole one and a half years we are in court in this trial, even more than one and a half years. Thank you, and with the best wishes for everybody, we adjourn.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.04 p.m.,
